doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Lena Horne, Gerry Mulligan and Basie's fixed arrangements
summary: He worked with Lena Horne and Mulligan, who kept changing things, unlike Basie whose arrangements stayed settled.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: Yeah, it sure did. But working with Brubeck and the whole Brubeck clan was just absolutely delightful. And then, after that, it’s been very notable. I’ve worked off and on for a few years with Lena Horne, who is one of my favorite all-time people in the world, not only just as an entertainer, but as a person, I love her. I’ve worked with Gerry Mulligan off and on for a couple of years, fascinating experience, I really dig Gerry. You know we’ve been good, close friends for a number of years and he was always remarkable to work with because you never knew what he was going to do. Same with Lena. You could rehearse the heck out of something, I mean have it down like this, and you get on stage and it’s no, no, no, we’re going to change that, we’re going to change this, let’s throw this over here, let’s do a stop time, then no, I want a little faster, no a little slower. You know all of a sudden it was well what were we spending all those days rehearsing for? Now we’re changing things. But that’s part of jazz, that’s part of jazz. That’s one thing that Basie did not do a great deal of was change things. Once that arrangement was settled the way it was, it stayed settled. The solos would change, I mean guys could change solos and do whatever they want, but if you had two chords to make
your statement, it’s quick. And once again it was the machine, it had to be like that. Otherwise you could have 18 anarchists up there on stage.
